title: It's going to be a slow recovery amid coronavirus: Citi chief strategist
description: Tobias Levkovich, Citi Chief U.S. Equity Strategist, joins "Closing Bell" to discuss the state of the markets.  Stocks surged on Wednesday after Sen. Bernie Sanders dropped out of the presidential race, relieving some of Wall Street's political concerns amid the economic crisis stemming from the coronavirus.  The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 779.71 points, or 3.4%, to close at 23,433.57. The S&P 500 climbed 3.4% to 2,749.98 while the Nasdaq Composite advanced 2.6% to 8,090.90. Hope the U.S. could start to turn a corner on the coronavirus outbreak in the near future also lifted equities.   Some of Sanders' policy proposals, including Medicare for All, raised concern among several business owners and investors who feared taxes would go up under his presidency. Wednesday's news puts former Vice President Joe Biden — who is seen by Wall Street as a more market-friendly candidate — closer to the Democratic nomination.  “Sanders' exit removes the tail risk of some of his policies, immediately sets up focus on Biden vs. Trump,” said Ed Mills, Washington policy strategist at Raymond James. “Biden's policies will get a new scrutiny now he is the presumptive nominee, but the truth of the matter is that the market will be looking towards Washington more to help the economy and much of the assistance matches his platform.”  For access to live and exclusive video from CNBC subscribe to CNBC PRO:  https://cnb.cx/2JdMwO7    » Subscribe to CNBC TV: https://cnb.cx/SubscribeCNBCtelevision » Subscribe to CNBC: https://cnb.cx/SubscribeCNBC » Subscribe to CNBC Classic: https://cnb.cx/SubscribeCNBCclassic   Turn to CNBC TV for the latest stock market news and analysis. asr.full_text: we've been telling investors for a while that we thought a 2,100 to 2,700 range was something to be thinking about. This is just over two and a half weeks ago when we put that out. So at this range kind of or the high end or just beyond that range, I would be a little bit more suspect here. There has been short squeezes. There has been some other positive news developments on the healthcare side. But we are concerned that people may have run a bit too hard on this thing because there's going to be a lot of bad news on the earnings flow. It's going to be a slow recovery when you come out of this. I don't think anybody with the right mind is going to be running around and doing what they were doing two, three months ago given fears around second outbreaks and other infections. We're all going to be a little bit more wary as we come out. Tobias, you at Citi have a really good real time indicator of sentiment and panic euphoria, all that kind of stuff, which helps sort of predict market action and activity. What are you seeing right now? So the last day we had with last Friday, we were we were still in panic territory, not deeply, but we were historically when we're there, we had was last Friday. We were still in panic territory. Not deeply, but we were, historically, when we're there, we get 18% rallies. But we really got that in, you know, here now over 20% rallies. So, it's come a little bit faster. Not entirely surprising, given how deep and how rapid the plunge was. But it's a little hard to chase that now. And I will tell you, the tone of conversations with people who have changed so yenteen every co people were literally asking me should i'd like i don't protect my my family infancy security perspective and now it's that they were off to the races were to be out of order back to work in a couple weeks and this is awesome meant to see kind of the whole state eight-year-old polar opposite of what we're hearing literally two and a half weeks ago. And that's a little bit worrying. Josh, the Russell 2000 in terms of year-to-date performance is some 20 percent still behind the NASDAQ, down close to 30 percent still. Does that make sense to you because of the risk of bankruptcies hidden within that index? Or do you think that's an opportunity? It does. The modern portfolio theorists would tell you that small caps outperform because the investor is taking more risk by owning them. Therefore, there should be a higher, there should be a quote premium return. And that's fine. It may come out over 30 and 40 year periods. But in acute economic disasters like this one, that is definitely not going to work. It's going to work against you. So it's not surprising that companies that have smaller market capitalizations also have more investors fretting over whether or not they'll be able to get financing. So it doesn't surprise me. I actually wanted to ask Tobias Lefkowitz your question. One of my favorite things that the Citi puts out is the economic surprise index. How cartoonish have the expectations become and how easy will it now be to beat them? And to your point about that swing from, should I buy a gun to, hey, this is amazing. We're going to be off to the races. That's a that's a psychological thing. That's like when you just narrowly avert a car accident, there's like an adrenaline rush that makes you feel alive. And I agree that that is gonna be tempered somewhat as the economic data continues to come out. But I'm curious. What is the surprise index telling us right now? So look, the expectations I don't think have come down to the way they should relative to what we're likely to see in the second quarter to a great degree in the U.S. We were kind of shut down for two weeks in March. We're going to be shut down pretty much all of April and maybe parts of May. And, you know, that just means very, very significant dropoffs. The service sector is 70 to 75 percent of the U.S. economy. And as opposed to being our strength, which it has been historically, in a world of work from home, shelter-in-place and social distancing, it now becomes your Achilles heel. So, I do think some of those numbers are easy to beat, but I'd be careful in trying to interpret that necessarily from a market trading perspective. In many respects, the economic surprise index is not exactly what people think it is. There's a six-week trailing set of data, and it's a six-week forward trailing data. I don't want to go into all the technical details. But it's not exactly the way it was described by many, many people on Wall Street who don't understand its construction. What I am fascinated is you said the behavioral aspect, Josh. And I would note two things. One, behavioral finance is really, really important to the way people were willing to pay for really worried if you are worried that you may have been a passenger in my car too many times if you are worried about close calls with accidents".
